summary: Describes network slicing for networks built from IETF technologies. It defines the term "IETF Network Slice", sets out general principles, and covers the framework for requesting and operating slices, their characteristics, and the system components and interfaces involved.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC gives network providers and customers shared terms for services that connect endpoints with performance commitments. It describes how a controller can turn a customer's request into settings for the provider's network.

questions: what is an ietf network slice
what is a network slice controller
subtitle: A shared framework for requesting connectivity with defined performance goals.

tldr.problem: Customers need network connectivity with performance commitments, while the term network slice has different meanings across standards work.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines an IETF Network Slice Service in terms of endpoints, connectivity constructs, and measurable objectives or expectations, then describes a controller that maps requests to network configuration.
tldr.outcome: It provides common terminology and a high-level framework. It does not define new protocols or detailed service interfaces.

today: RFC 9543 is an Informational RFC published in March 2024. Its metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; the document provides terminology and a framework, not new protocols or detailed interfaces.

sections.title: The IETF Network Slice Service
sections.content:
An IETF Network Slice provides connectivity between endpoints over a shared network, with commitments about network resources. The IETF Network Slice Service is the service a customer requests; the slice is the provider's implementation of that service.

The RFC limits its scope to networks built from IETF technologies. It supplies terminology and a framework for discussing interfaces and technologies, rather than defining those interfaces or selecting one implementation.
sections.plainLanguage: The customer asks for connectivity and performance goals. The provider chooses how to configure its shared network to meet that request.

sections.title: Endpoints and Connectivity
sections.content:
A service is described with Service Demarcation Points (SDPs), connectivity constructs between groups of SDPs, and objectives for traffic sent from each SDP. An SDP is the point where the provider delivers service to the customer.

The RFC defines point-to-point, point-to-multipoint, and any-to-any connectivity constructs. They describe whether one sender reaches one receiver, several receivers, or any receiver in a group.
sections.plainLanguage: A service description names where traffic enters and leaves the service, and which endpoints can communicate. It can describe a link between two endpoints or communication involving a group.

sections.title: Measurable Objectives and Expectations
sections.content:
Service Level Objectives (SLOs) set measurable targets based on indicators such as bandwidth, latency, delay variation, packet loss, and availability. A customer can measure whether the provider meets an SLO.

Service Level Expectations (SLEs) describe requests that customers generally cannot measure directly, such as isolation, security, or geographic restrictions. SLOs and SLEs together describe the service agreement.
sections.plainLanguage: An SLO is a promise the customer can check with measurements. An SLE is a service request, such as keeping traffic separate, that the customer may not be able to verify directly.

sections.title: The Network Slice Controller
sections.content:
The customer expresses what service is needed through the IETF Network Slice Service Interface. The Network Slice Controller (NSC) receives this abstract request and maps it to capabilities and configuration for the provider's network.

The NSC can also collect telemetry and assess performance against SLOs. It communicates with network controllers through technology-specific interfaces; the RFC leaves the detailed service interface out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The NSC translates the customer's goals into instructions that the provider's network can use. It can also collect measurements and compare them with the requested objectives.

sections.title: Realizing and Isolating Slices
sections.content:
The provider may realize a service using filtered network topologies and network resource partitions. The RFC describes a process in which the NSC checks capabilities, receives a request, maps it to network resources, and creates or extends a partition.

Isolation is a service requirement that can be supported through resource partitioning, traffic separation, capacity planning, or other measures. The RFC notes that customers may not be able to observe isolation directly.
sections.plainLanguage: The provider reserves or configures network resources to support the requested service. The exact technology is a provider choice, and isolation may be difficult for a customer to verify unless service performance changes.
